beats.say: Welcome the child in one warm sentence, then say what today is about: they already know numbers with three digits; today there is one more column, and three jobs - read a 4-digit number, write it, and break it into parts. Two sentences at most, then move straight to the chart.

board.text: Read it - write it - break it apart

beats.say: A digit is one of the ten symbols 0 to 9; a number is built from digits. What a digit is worth depends on where it sits. Show the empty place value chart and ask the child to predict which column is worth the most before telling them.

board.text: A number is built from digits

board.label: The column worth the most is the ___

ask.prompt: Look at the chart. Which column is worth the most - the left one or the right one?
ask.lookFor: The left one (thousands). A good answer says why: the places get bigger as you go left.
ask.onMiss: Do not tell them yet. Put one counter in the thousands column and one in the ones column and ask which pile you would rather have. Then re-ask.

beats.say: Build the number with place-value counters. A counter is worth different amounts in different trays - that is the whole idea. Place the thousand counters and the hundred counters first.

board.text: Th - H - T - U = thousands, hundreds, tens, ones

beats.say: Now the tens and the ones. Then read the digits off the chart, column by column, left to right.

board.label: The digit 3 sits in the ___ place

ask.prompt: Reading the chart from left to right, which place does the digit 3 sit in?
ask.lookFor: Hundreds. The child should be able to point to the column, not only name it.
ask.onMiss: Ask them to name the four columns from the left, one at a time, then count along to the 3.

beats.say: The most common mix-up: treating a digit as only its face. In 6423 the 4 looks like a four, but it is worth something different. Put the two ideas side by side. Do not call it a mistake; just show the test: if the 4 meant four ones, the parts would add up to the wrong number.

board.title: Place value
board.text: what it is worth in 6423: 4 hundreds

ask.prompt: In 6423, is the digit 4 worth 4, 40 or 400? What tells you?
ask.lookFor: 400, because the 4 is in the hundreds column (4 x 100). Listen for the reason, not just the number.
ask.onMiss: Go back to the chart: ask which column the 4 is in, and what ONE counter in that column is worth. Then re-ask.

beats.say: Say the rule in the child's own words after you state it: a digit's value is the digit times the value of its place. Then write 6423 as the sum of its parts so they see the rule in use.

board.text: value of a digit = the digit × its place

beats.say: Where the rule needs care: zero. When a column has nothing, zero holds the place open. Show 4040 with its empty hundreds and ones, and what happens if the zeros are left out.

board.text: leave the zeros out and 4040 shrinks to 44

ask.prompt: Write 'four thousand and forty' in figures. How many digits does it have, and what is in the hundreds column?
ask.lookFor: 4040 - four digits, with 0 in the hundreds column. A common slip is 440 or 4400.
ask.onMiss: Ask them to say the four columns out loud: how many thousands, hundreds, tens, ones? Fill the hundreds with 0 together.

beats.say: Now the method for breaking a number apart (expanded form): name the column, write that digit's full value, then join the values with plus signs. Work 4567 line by line, then ask about the 5.

ask.onMiss: Ask which column the 5 is in and what each counter there is worth, then multiply.

beats.say: Their turn, on a fresh chart: 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 8 tens, 4 ones. Ask them to write the number AND break it apart. Let them work it out; do not give hints until they are stuck.

ask.prompt: Look at this chart. What number is it, and how do you break it apart?
ask.lookFor: 3084 and 3000 + 0 + 80 + 4. The zero in the hundreds must be kept.
ask.onMiss: Name the columns from the left and ask what is in each. If the hundreds are dropped, return to 'zero holds the place'.

beats.say: Close with a fresh case that tests whether the idea transfers: the same digit in a different place. Ask for the reason, not only the number.

ask.prompt: In 5764, what is the 5 worth? Why is that different from the 5 in 4567?
ask.lookFor: 5000, because it is in the thousands column now. The reason is the place, not the digit.
ask.onMiss: Put the number on the chart and ask which column the 5 sits in this time, then re-ask the reason.
